title: Swords into Plowshares: The Mountain of the LORD
summary: In the last days the mountain of the LORD's house will be raised above all others, and many nations will stream to it to learn God's ways. He will judge between them, and they will beat their swords into plowshares, each person sitting safely under his own vine and fig tree. God will gather the lame and the outcast into a strong nation and reign over them in Zion. But first Zion must writhe like a woman in labor, go to Babylon, and be redeemed there, and God will turn the nations gathered against her into sheaves on the threshing floor.
story: Chapter 3 ended with Zion plowed like a field and the temple mount a wooded ridge. Chapter 4 begins with the same mountain raised higher than every other, with the nations streaming to it. The juxtaposition is deliberate: the judgment of chapter 3 is real, but it is not the end. This chapter and the next form the hope section of Micah's second cycle. It moves from a vision of the far future (verses 1 to 5) through God's promise to gather his scattered people (verses 6 to 8) to the painful path by which Zion will get there: labor pains, exile to Babylon, and rescue (verses 9 to 13). Chapter 5 will continue with the promise of a ruler from Bethlehem.
historical:
Micah 4:1-3 appears almost word for word in Isaiah 2:2-4. Isaiah and Micah were contemporaries in eighth-century Judah, and scholars have long debated the relationship. Some think Micah borrowed from Isaiah, some that Isaiah borrowed from Micah, and some that both drew on an older prophetic oracle known in Jerusalem. Others think the passage was added to both books by later editors. Micah's version adds verse 4 (the vine and fig tree) and verse 5, which fit his rural setting.

Verse 10 names Babylon as the place where Zion will go and be rescued. In Micah's day Assyria was the great power, and Babylon was a subject city, though often a rebellious one; its king Merodach-baladan sent envoys to Hezekiah (Isaiah 39, 2 Kings 20:12-19), and Isaiah warned then that Judah's treasures and descendants would be carried to Babylon. Many scholars regard verse 10 as a later addition from the time of the exile after 587 or 586 BC. Others argue that an eighth-century prophet aware of Babylon's ambitions could have spoken of it, especially in light of Isaiah's similar prediction. The Babylonian exile and the return under Cyrus in 539/538 BC fulfilled the pattern of going to Babylon and being redeemed there.
cultural:
Temples in the ancient Near East were often built on high places, and mountains were thought of as places where heaven and earth met. The vision of the LORD's mountain raised above all others means that the God of Israel will be recognized as supreme over all gods and nations. Instead of armies marching up to attack Jerusalem, the nations come in pilgrimage to learn. The "law" that goes out from Zion is torah, instruction, the teaching of God's ways.

Plowshares were the metal blades of plows, and pruning hooks were blades used to trim vines. Beating weapons into farm tools pictures the end of war and the redirection of iron and bronze from killing to cultivating. The image of each person under his own vine and fig tree (verse 4) was a proverbial picture of peace and security, used of Solomon's reign (1 Kings 4:25) and in Zechariah 3:10. It meant a family living on its own land, eating its own produce, with no enemy to take it away, the opposite of the land seizures Micah condemned in chapter 2. The "watchtower of the flock" (verse 8) translates Migdal-eder, a place near Bethlehem mentioned in Genesis 35:21. Threshing (verse 13) separated grain from husk by trampling or beating; an ox with bronze hooves would crush everything on the threshing floor.
literary: The chapter is a collection of oracles linked by the themes of Zion and the nations. Verses 1 to 5 are a vision introduced by "In the last days" and closed by a confession of loyalty: though the peoples walk in the name of their gods, "we will walk in the name of the LORD our God forever and ever". Verses 6 to 8 are introduced by "On that day" and gather the lame and outcast. Verses 9 to 13 contain three oracles each beginning with "now" (verses 9 and 11, and 5:1, which Hebrew Bibles number as 4:14), each describing present distress followed by future deliverance. The image of a woman in labor (verses 9 and 10) carries both pain and hope, since labor ends in birth. The chapter moves from peace among the nations to the nations gathered in hostility, showing that the peaceful future comes through conflict and judgment.

outline.t: The nations stream to the mountain of the LORD
Swords into plowshares, each under his own vine
We will walk in the name of the LORD
The lame and outcast gathered; dominion restored to Zion
Zion in labor: to Babylon and redeemed
The nations gathered like sheaves for threshing

doctrines.note: The chapter pictures God's reign extending to all nations, who come to learn his ways and submit to his judgment. "The LORD will rule over them in Mount Zion from that day and forever" (verse 7).

The nations come to Zion not as conquerors but as learners: "He will teach us His ways, so that we may walk in His paths" (verse 2). God's purpose for Israel was always connected to blessing all peoples.
Micah's hope includes the end of war and the security of every family on its own land. It rests on God's word: "the mouth of the LORD of Hosts has spoken" (verse 4).
God will redeem Zion from the hand of her enemies, even in Babylon (verse 10). He gathers the lame and the outcast, choosing the weak to become a strong nation (verses 6 and 7).

words.note: Torah, instruction or law. In verse 2 it goes out from Zion to the nations. Torah is broader than a legal code; it is God's teaching about how to live. The nations come not merely to be ruled but to be taught.

Et, plowshare, the iron blade of a plow. Joel 3:10 reverses this image, calling the nations to beat their plowshares into swords for the battle of God's judgment. Micah and Isaiah describe what lies beyond that battle: weapons turned into tools for feeding people.

Tsala, to limp. "The lame" in verses 6 and 7 are literally those who limp. The same verb describes Jacob limping after wrestling with God (Genesis 32:31). God builds his strong nation not from the powerful but from the injured and the outcast.

Ga'al, to redeem. The kinsman-redeemer in Israel's law bought back a relative's land or freedom (Leviticus 25:25, Ruth 4). Here God acts as Zion's redeemer, rescuing her from her enemies in Babylon. The word pictures God as a close relative who pays to restore.

christ: The New Testament sees the vision of Micah 4 beginning to be fulfilled in the gospel. Jesus told his disciples that repentance and forgiveness would be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem (Luke 24:47), and in Acts the word of the Lord goes out from Jerusalem to Judea, Samaria, and the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8). The nations who come to learn God's ways find that teaching in Jesus, who invited all to learn from him (Matthew 11:29). Christians differ on how the full vision will be fulfilled: some expect a literal future reign of Christ from Jerusalem, others see its fulfillment in the church and the new creation. All agree that the peace Micah describes, the end of war and every person secure, is the peace Christ brings in its fullness when he returns and God makes all things new (Revelation 21).

hard.q: How can Micah say nations will beat their swords into plowshares when war continues?
hard.a: Micah places this vision "in the last days" (verse 1), a phrase pointing to the future when God's purposes are complete, not to a program that nations can achieve by treaties alone. Interpreters differ on how the fulfillment unfolds. Premillennialists expect a future period when Christ reigns on earth and war ceases. Amillennialists and postmillennialists see the vision beginning now, as the gospel spreads and peace takes root among Christ's people, and completed in the new creation. Others emphasize that the passage calls God's people to live now as citizens of that coming peace. The chapter itself holds the vision alongside a realistic picture of present conflict (verses 9 to 13), so it does not deny the reality of war. It declares that war will not have the last word.

questions: The nations come to Zion saying, "He will teach us His ways". What would it look like for you to come to God as a learner rather than with your own agenda?
Micah pictures peace as every person under his own vine and fig tree, with no one to frighten him. What would that kind of security mean for the people around you who lack it?
God gathers the lame and the outcast and makes them a strong nation. How does that shape the way a church should see those the world overlooks?
